body:
Meaning of base level

The base level of erosion is the limiting elevation towards which a river tends to erode its channel.

A river flowing from a higher elevation to a lower elevation possesses energy derived from gravity. This energy allows it to erode its channel and transport sediment. As its gradient decreases, its capacity for further vertical erosion may also decrease.

Ultimate and local base levels

Ultimate base level

Sea level is regarded as the ultimate base level for rivers draining into the oceans. It provides the general downstream reference towards which their channels develop.

Local or temporary base level

A river may encounter an intermediate limit that controls erosion within a particular section of its course. This is called a local base level.

Examples include:

  • The water surface of a lake into which a river flows.
  • A reservoir created by a dam.
  • The level of a main river where a tributary joins it.
  • A resistant rock obstruction controlling upstream channel elevation.

Local base levels may change when lakes fill with sediment, dams are removed, rock barriers are eroded or the elevation of a receiving river changes.

River longitudinal profile

The longitudinal profile of a river represents the variation in channel elevation from its source to its mouth.

A well-adjusted river profile is generally concave upwards, with steeper gradients in its upper course and gentler gradients towards its lower course.

The actual profile may contain waterfalls, rapids and other irregularities caused by rock resistance, tectonic movements or changes in base level.

Effects of changes in base level

Lowering of base level

When base level falls, a river may acquire a steeper gradient relative to its outlet. This can increase its capacity for vertical erosion and cause renewed channel incision.

The relative lowering of base level may result from a fall in sea level, uplift of the land drained by the river or lowering of a local base level.

Raising of base level

When base level rises, the downstream gradient may decrease and the river may deposit part of its sediment load.

A reservoir provides a familiar example. As flowing river water enters the relatively still reservoir, its velocity decreases and sediment tends to accumulate.

River rejuvenation

Rejuvenation refers to the renewal or intensification of river erosion following a change that increases its erosive capacity relative to the existing channel conditions.

It commonly occurs after tectonic uplift or a fall in base level. Increased river discharge under changed climatic conditions can also contribute to renewed erosion, depending on the accompanying change in sediment supply.

Features associated with rejuvenation include:

  • River terraces: Remnants of former valley floors or floodplains left above the present river channel after renewed incision.
  • Incised or entrenched meanders: Existing river bends that become deeply cut into the underlying land.
  • Knickpoints: Abrupt breaks in the river's longitudinal slope, sometimes expressed as waterfalls or rapids.

Base level is a control on river erosion, not a guarantee that a river will reach a perfectly level surface or cease all erosion and sediment movement.

Prelims focus

  • Sea level is the ultimate base level for ocean-draining rivers.
  • Lakes and reservoirs can act as local base levels.
  • A graded longitudinal profile is generally concave upwards.
  • Lowering of base level can renew vertical erosion.
  • River terraces and incised meanders may indicate rejuvenation.
  • Trap: Raising a river's base level generally favours deposition rather than renewed downward erosion.

[References: Virginia Tech, Introduction to Earth Science, Water chapter, Stream Equilibrium and Base Level discussion; INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Geomorphology, Module 18, Interruptions of the Cycle of Erosion (Tectonics, Climatic and Base Level Changes); Michael E. Ritter, The Physical Environment, Stream Gradation. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

title: Base Level of Erosion and River Rejuvenation

body:
Davis and the geographical cycle

The American geographer William Morris Davis developed a classical model of landscape evolution known as the geographical cycle or cycle of erosion. His major work, The Geographical Cycle, was published in 1899.

Davis explained landscape development through the interaction of 3 elements:

  • Structure: The geological composition and arrangement of rocks.
  • Process: The geomorphic processes acting upon the landscape.
  • Stage: The degree of landscape development through time.

His idealised cycle assumes that land is uplifted and subsequently undergoes a prolonged period of erosion under comparatively stable environmental and tectonic conditions.

Stages of the Davisian cycle

Youth

Following uplift, rivers actively cut down into the land. Valleys are relatively narrow and deep, with steep slopes, waterfalls and rapids. Floodplains are generally poorly developed. Valley incision can increase local relief even while the land is undergoing erosion.

Maturity

The drainage system becomes more developed. Continued erosion widens valleys, and lateral erosion becomes increasingly important. Floodplains become more extensive, and rivers may develop pronounced meanders. Relief becomes less rugged as interfluves, the areas between neighbouring valleys, are gradually worn down.

Old age

Prolonged denudation produces a landscape with gentle gradients and low relief. Rivers commonly flow through broad valleys and extensive floodplains. In the ideal model, the land approaches a nearly level erosional surface called a peneplain.

Resistant residual hills may remain above the peneplain. Such isolated remnants are known as monadnocks.

Limitations of the cycle concept

The Davisian cycle is a useful historical model for understanding gradual landscape transformation, but real landscapes do not necessarily pass through its stages in a fixed order.

Uplift can continue while erosion is taking place. Climate may change, sea level may rise or fall, and extreme events may interrupt gradual development. Renewed uplift or lowering of base level can also produce rejuvenation before an earlier cycle has reached its theoretical final stage.

Youth, maturity and old age describe idealised stages of geomorphic development. They do not specify fixed ages in years.

Dynamic equilibrium

The concept of dynamic equilibrium explains how a landscape or landform can maintain relatively stable overall characteristics even while physical processes continue operating.

For example, river erosion, sediment transportation and deposition continue in a drainage system. If these processes remain approximately balanced over time, the general channel profile may remain relatively stable.

Graded river

A graded river has adjusted its gradient and channel characteristics so that its sediment-transporting capacity is approximately balanced with the sediment supplied to it over a relevant period.

A graded river may still transport sediment, erode its banks and undergo local or seasonal changes. Its equilibrium is dynamic rather than an absence of activity.

Adjustment to disturbance

If sediment supply increases substantially without a corresponding increase in transporting capacity, sediment may accumulate within the channel. If transporting capacity increases relative to sediment supply, renewed erosion may occur.

Similarly, a coastline can remain relatively stable when sediment gains and losses are balanced, even though waves and currents continually move material.

Cycle and equilibrium compared

AspectCycle of erosionDynamic equilibrium
Main emphasisLandscape transformation through stagesContinuing adjustment among processes
Role of timeCentral to the developmental sequenceBalance evaluated over a relevant period
Landscape stabilityIdealised approach towards low reliefRelative stability despite ongoing activity
Effect of disturbanceMay interrupt or renew a cycleMay cause adjustment towards a new balance

Prelims focus

  • William Morris Davis is associated with the geographical cycle of erosion.
  • The Geographical Cycle was published in 1899.
  • The ideal sequence is youth, maturity and old age.
  • A peneplain is a nearly level erosional surface.
  • A monadnock is a resistant residual hill.
  • Trap: Dynamic equilibrium does not mean that erosion, transportation and deposition have stopped.

[References: William Morris Davis, The Geographical Cycle, The Geographical Journal, 1899, Vol. 14, pp. 481-504; INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, Geomorphology, Modules 16 and 18, Davisian Cycle and Interruptions of the Cycle of Erosion; Michael E. Ritter, The Physical Environment, Stream Gradation, The Davisian Cycle and The Graded Stream sections. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

title: The Cycle of Erosion and Dynamic Equilibrium

body:
Meaning of a geomorphic hazard

A geomorphic hazard arises from a physical process that changes the Earth's surface and has the potential to harm people, infrastructure, livelihoods or the environment.

Geomorphic hazards may develop gradually, as in long-term shoreline erosion, or rapidly, as in a landslide or severe storm-related coastal inundation.

Hazard, exposure, vulnerability and risk

  • Hazard: A potentially damaging process or event.
  • Exposure: The presence of people, buildings or other assets in an area affected by the hazard.
  • Vulnerability: The degree to which exposed people or assets are susceptible to harm.
  • Risk: The potential for adverse consequences arising from the interaction of hazard, exposure and vulnerability.

A steep and unstable coastal cliff may present a natural hazard. Construction near its retreating edge increases exposure, while weak foundations or inadequate protection may increase vulnerability.

A natural process becomes a major disaster risk when people and valuable assets are exposed to it and are vulnerable to its effects.

Major coastal hazards

Coastal erosion

Repeated wave attack, strong currents or inadequate sediment supply may remove beaches and coastal land. Erosion can undermine buildings, roads and other infrastructure close to the shoreline.

Storm surge

A storm surge is an abnormal rise in coastal water level associated with a storm, particularly a tropical cyclone. Strong winds pushing seawater towards the coast are its principal cause, while low atmospheric pressure also contributes.

The actual water level reached during a storm depends on the surge, astronomical tide, waves and local coastal conditions. Shallow coastal waters and low-lying land can increase the extent of inundation.

Tsunami

A tsunami is a series of long waves generated by the sudden displacement of a large volume of water. Undersea earthquakes are the most common cause, although submarine landslides and volcanic activity can also generate tsunamis.

Tsunamis can inundate low-lying coastal land, erode beaches and redistribute substantial quantities of sediment.

PhenomenonPrimary generating mechanism
Ordinary wavesWind transferring energy to water
Astronomical tidesGravitational effects of Moon and Sun
Storm surgeStorm winds and atmospheric pressure changes
TsunamiSudden displacement of a large water volume

Long-term coastal inundation and subsidence

Relative sea-level rise and land subsidence can increase flooding and promote the inland movement of coastal waters. Low-lying deltas are particularly sensitive where sediment accumulation fails to maintain land elevation relative to rising water levels.

Landslides and other slope failures

A landslide is the downslope movement of a mass of rock, debris or soil under gravity. Slope failure occurs when the forces promoting movement exceed the resistance of the slope material.

Factors increasing slope instability

  • Steep slopes and weak or fractured rocks.
  • Heavy rainfall and water saturation.
  • Earthquake shaking.
  • Removal of support at the base of a slope by rivers, waves or excavation.
  • Uncontrolled slope cutting and additional loading.
  • Loss of stabilising vegetation in susceptible areas.

Rainfall can increase the weight of slope material and raise water pressure within soil and rock pores, reducing resistance to movement. An earthquake may supply the additional force needed to initiate failure.

Prelims focus

  • Storm surges are mainly associated with strong storm winds.
  • Tsunamis result from sudden large-scale water displacement.
  • Mass wasting is driven directly by gravity.
  • Heavy rainfall and slope undercutting can initiate landslides.
  • Land subsidence can worsen coastal inundation.
  • Trap: Hazard and disaster risk are not identical; exposure and vulnerability influence risk.

[References: NCERT, Class 7, Our Environment, 2018-19 edition, Chapter 5, Waves section, pp. 33-35; NCERT, Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Geomorphic Processes, Mass Movements section; INCOIS, Indian Tsunami Early Warning System, About and About Storm Surge sections; IPCC, Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, Chapter 3, Sea Level Rise and Extreme Sea Levels section. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

title: Geomorphic Hazards: Coastal Erosion, Flooding and Slope Failure

body:
Planning according to geomorphic conditions

Hazard-sensitive planning involves identifying natural processes that can damage settlements and infrastructure and incorporating this understanding into decisions about land use, construction and environmental management.

The objective is not necessarily to stop every natural geomorphic process. It is to reduce exposure and vulnerability while maintaining the functions of rivers, slopes and coastal environments.

Coastal planning and protection

Hazard mapping and land-use planning

Shoreline change maps identify coastal stretches experiencing erosion, accretion or relative stability. Coastal inundation maps indicate areas that may be affected by elevated seawater levels during hazardous events.

These maps help planners identify unsuitable locations for new construction, establish appropriate setbacks from unstable shorelines, protect evacuation routes and locate essential infrastructure in safer areas.

Natural protective features

  • Beaches and offshore bars: Can absorb or dissipate part of the energy of incoming waves.
  • Coastal dunes: Act as natural barriers and sediment reserves.
  • Mangroves: Trap sediment, stabilise suitable muddy shores and reduce the energy of waves and water flows.
  • Coastal wetlands: Provide space for floodwater and sediment accumulation.

These natural features reduce certain coastal risks but do not provide complete protection against every storm or tsunami.

Engineering and accommodation measures

MeasurePurpose
SeawallProtect coastal land from direct wave attack
GroyneInterrupt longshore sediment movement
Beach nourishmentAdd compatible sediment to replenish a beach
Elevated constructionReduce vulnerability to inundation
Coastal setbackKeep vulnerable development away from hazardous shoreline areas
Managed retreatRelocate exposed development from areas of unacceptable risk

Protection measures must account for neighbouring shores. A structure that interrupts sediment transport may protect one location while increasing erosion elsewhere. Therefore, coastal management should consider the wider sediment system instead of treating each beach independently.

Planning in landslide-prone areas

Landslide susceptibility maps identify areas where terrain conditions make slope failure more likely. They support decisions regarding settlements, roads and other infrastructure.

Risk reduction measures include avoiding unstable slopes, regulating excavation and construction, providing proper drainage, retaining stabilising vegetation and adopting suitable slope protection where necessary.

Susceptibility indicates the relative tendency of a location to experience slope failure. It does not, by itself, predict the exact time at which a landslide will occur.

Indian institutions associated with geomorphic hazard assessment

  • National Centre for Coastal Research (NCCR): Studies coastal processes, shoreline changes, coastal erosion and related coastal management problems.
  • Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS): Operates the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre and provides ocean-related hazard information.
  • Geological Survey of India (GSI): Undertakes geological investigations and landslide susceptibility mapping.

These activities support hazard assessment and preparedness. Scientific warnings and maps must be combined with appropriate land-use planning, construction practices and public preparedness to reduce disaster risk.

Integrated understanding of landscapes

Coastal and inland landforms are connected through the movement of water and sediment. Tectonic uplift and climate influence erosion in uplands. Rivers transport sediments downstream, while marine processes redistribute those sediments along the coast.

Changes in base level, sediment supply or wave energy can disturb an existing geomorphic balance. The resulting adjustments may build landforms in one location and create hazards in another.

Understanding these relationships helps explain why river valleys, deltas, beaches and unstable slopes require different but interconnected approaches to planning.

Prelims focus

  • Shoreline change maps distinguish erosion, accretion and relative stability.
  • Beach nourishment adds sediment rather than interrupting its movement.
  • Mangroves and dunes provide natural coastal protection.
  • NCCR is associated with coastal research and shoreline assessment.
  • INCOIS operates India's Tsunami Early Warning Centre.
  • Trap: Landslide susceptibility mapping does not provide an exact prediction of the time of slope failure.

[References: National Centre for Coastal Research, National Assessment of Shoreline Changes along Indian Coast, July 2018, Preface and Sections 1 and 4, historical assessment for 1990-2016; INCOIS, Indian Tsunami Early Warning System, About and Early Warnings sections; Geological Survey of India, Landslide Hazard, Aims and Objectives; IPCC, Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate, 2019, Chapter 4 and FAQ 4.1; IPCC, Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability, Cross-Chapter Paper 2, Section CCP2.3. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]
